players.product: AI GPU cloud (liquid + air-cooled data centers; 5 GW secured power, target 150k GPUs)

quarterly_data.signal: Fiscal Q2 FY2026 total revenue was $184.7 million, down 23% on the prior quarter, mainly because Bitcoin mining revenue fell: fewer bitcoin were mined as the AI transition lowered operating hashrate, and average Bitcoin prices were lower. AI cloud revenue grew as new GPUs were commissioned at Prince George, which partly offset the decline. Adjusted EBITDA declined on the lower mining revenue. The quarter carried $219.4 million of non-cash and non-recurring items: unrealized losses on prepaid forwards and cap calls tied to the convertible notes, plus a one-time debt conversion inducement expense. It also included $31.8 million of mining hardware impairment linked to the AI cloud transition (vs $16 million in the prior period) and a $192.5 million income tax benefit. CFO Anthony Lewis said IREN ended January with 'a strong cash position of $2.8 billion'.
quarterly_data.figure: Total revenue $184.7 million, down 23% on the prior quarter; $31.8 million mining hardware impairment; $192.5 million income tax benefit; cash position of $2.8 billion at end of January

quarterly_data.signal: Contracted ARR and 2026 deployment target: IREN has 'approximately $2.3 billion of annualized revenue run rate under contract, including around $0.4 billion at Prince George'. Management expects the Prince George amount to increase over the coming weeks as it finalizes negotiations for the remaining capacity there; co-CEO Daniel Roberts described Prince George as 'just under $0.5 billion of ARR now under contract'. IREN expects to deliver 140,000 GPUs by the end of 2026, which supports its targeted $3.4 billion ARR by the end of calendar 2026. The additional 40,000 GPUs expected at Mackenzie equate to around $1 billion of ARR. Capacity at Mackenzie and Canal Flats will ramp progressively over the year, and customers remain 'very willing to make significant prepayments' for it. Revenue from the Microsoft contract will come online progressively over the year, with initial revenues expected to start in Q2. Management stressed that 'demand is not the limiting factor' and said the $3.4 billion ARR target uses only around 10% of its 4.5 gigawatts of secured grid-connected power.
quarterly_data.figure: approximately $2.3 billion of ARR under contract (around $0.4 billion at Prince George); 140,000 GPUs by the end of 2026; $3.4 billion ARR target by end of calendar 2026; additional 40,000 GPUs = around $1 billion of ARR

capex.display: approximately $2.3 billion of annualized revenue run rate under contract

quarterly_data.signal: Capital and capex: IREN secured underwriting commitments for $3.6 billion of GPU financing, a delayed-draw term loan from Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan that amortizes in full over its 5-year term. The loan is secured against the GPUs and Microsoft's contracted cash flows, with interest expected to be less than 6%. Together with Microsoft's $1.9 billion in prepayments, it covers 95% of the GPU-related CapEx for Horizons 1 through 4; Roberts put the average interest rate at around 3% once prepayments are factored in. Financial year-to-date, IREN has secured $9.2 billion from customer prepayments, convertible notes (including the $2.3 billion issued in December), GPU leasing arrangements and the dedicated Microsoft GPU financing. The CFO's capex breakdown: $5.8 billion of compute CapEx for Microsoft plus approximately $3 billion of data center CapEx (a material amount already incurred or committed); with the GPU financing and balance-sheet cash, 'all of the Microsoft related CapEx for the compute and DC' is spoken for. The remaining ARR-target expansion at Prince George and Mackenzie needs circa $3 billion of CapEx; a material amount of that has already been incurred and financed through lease-based financing. Next financing priorities are data center financing for Horizons 1 through 4 once they come online, plus select corporate-level facilities.
quarterly_data.figure: $3.6 billion GPU financing at less than 6%; Microsoft $1.9 billion prepayments; 95% of GPU related CapEx for Horizons 1 through 4 covered; $9.2 billion secured financial year-to-date; $5.8 billion compute CapEx for Microsoft; circa $3 billion CapEx for the Prince George / Mackenzie expansion

quarterly_data.signal: Secured power: IREN secured a new 1.6 gigawatt data center campus in Oklahoma, a very large site in the Southwest Power Pool immediately adjacent to a major utility substation, with low-latency connectivity to major network exchanges and a ramp schedule starting in 2028. The site takes total secured power to over 4.5 gigawatts and extends IREN's US pipeline beyond ERCOT. IREN also cited 810 megawatts of operating air-cooled data centers and 3.6 gigawatts of greenfield data center sites. On ERCOT's new batch study process, management believes Sweetwater 1 and 2 would be included in batch 0, which would mean the full 2 gigawatts is secured; the interconnection agreement was signed in 2023. Sweetwater 1 remains on track to energize in Q2, with full bulk substations capable of 1.4 gigawatts, and procurement and civil works are underway for the first phase of Sweetwater data centers. Roberts: 'time to power is critical, but time to data centers is actually the more limiting factor.'
quarterly_data.figure: new 1.6 gigawatt Oklahoma site; total secured power over 4.5 gigawatts; 810 megawatts of operating data centers; Sweetwater 1 energization in Q2 (1.4 gigawatts); full 2 gigawatts at Sweetwater secured

quarterly_data.signal: Build progress: at Prince George (British Columbia), data center fit-outs for air-cooled NVIDIA B200 and B300 GPUs are complete and are waiting for the remaining GPUs on order. At Mackenzie and Canal Flats, teams are preparing the sites for AI cloud expansion with the same playbook used at Prince George ('ASICs are coming out of those data centers and GPUs are going in'). At Childress, construction across Horizons 1 to 4 is on schedule to meet Microsoft's GPU deployment timelines. Management said the long-lead procurement and skilled-labor constraints seen across the industry are manageable for IREN because it builds continuously and has a team of over 2,000 people. It named the pace of construction, not power or capital, as the current constraint on the phased Sweetwater build-out.

Demand and pricing: 'demand is not the constraint for us.' IREN is in multiple advanced negotiations for larger-scale deployments with hyperscale and non-hyperscale counterparties. Hyperscalers and AI enterprises are increasingly focused on air-cooled GPUs because they deploy faster, which suits IREN's 810 megawatts of operating air-cooled data centers. Customers are more open to longer tenures than before, seeing 'a long-dated supply-demand imbalance', and continue to make prepayments. IREN keeps signing contracts for both new and prior-generation GPUs. According to management, newer chips go mostly to training while older ones shift toward inference. Chief Commercial Officer Kent Draper said there is 'an undersupply relative to demand' and that A100s, more than 5 years old, are 'still effectively 100% utilized across the industry'. He added that IREN expects chips to stay economically useful beyond its contract lengths, including the 5-year Microsoft contract.
quarterly_data.figure: older-generation GPUs (A100s more than 5 years old) still effectively 100% utilized

quarterly_data.signal: Strategy: IREN prefers AI cloud to colocation because power, and above all data center capacity, is scarce. Roberts said every incremental 200 megawatts can deliver either '$300 million-ish through a co-location or multiples of that in the billions under a cloud contract', though IREN would still pursue a compelling colocation deal. Most demand is bare-metal from hyperscalers and large AI firms, and software is a small share; even so, one contract under negotiation is 'a multibillion-dollar contract where we need to bring a software solution'. Asked about NVIDIA credit backstops for neoclouds, Roberts said it is 'a safe assumption' that IREN is having 'very similar, if not exact same dialogue' with all these counterparties about structures such as equity investments, credit backstops and offtake agreements.
quarterly_data.figure: every incremental 200 megawatts: $300 million-ish via co-location vs multiples of that in the billions under a cloud contract
